messages.text: I ran into an old high school friend yesterday. He asked why I wasn’t at the reunion.
It sounds like the question brought up some feelings or memories for you. How did you feel in that moment when he asked? Did you have a particular reason for not attending the reunion?
It just made me feel stupid, like I should’ve gone. I said I wasn’t sure it was my thing, but really—I didn’t think anyone would care if I showed up.

It’s understandable to feel that way, especially if you were worried about being overlooked. Sometimes those thoughts can make social events feel more risky than they really are. What do you think might have happened if you had gone?
I probably would’ve just stood there like a ghost, saying the wrong things. I always do.

It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of self-consciousness about how you come across to others. Those feelings can make it hard to imagine positive outcomes. Have there been times when social interactions went better than you expected?
There was this one time at a work thing years ago—people seemed to listen when I spoke, but it was probably just politeness.

It’s possible politeness played a role, but it also means you were engaging enough for others to respond. That moment shows you can connect, even if self-doubt makes it hard to trust it. Would you like to explore what helped you feel heard in that situation?
It’s not just the reunion. It’s that same old feeling from school—like I was background noise. And now it’s like I never left that version of myself behind.

It sounds like those old experiences are still shaping how you see yourself today. Feeling stuck in that “background” role can be heavy, especially when it follows you into adulthood. Would you like to talk about how we might challenge that old narrative?
I want to believe I’m more than that quiet girl who got ignored, but it’s hard. That version of me feels more real than anything else.

It’s understandable that the long-standing image feels more “real,” especially if it was reinforced over time. We can work on building evidence that supports a fuller, more balanced picture of you. What’s one small moment recently when you felt even slightly seen or valued?
I don’t know… maybe when my roommate thanked me for taking out the trash? It’s silly, but she said it made her week easier.

That’s not silly at all—it’s a clear example of your actions having a positive impact on someone. Small moments like that can be seeds for a new self-story. How would it feel to start collecting these moments over time as proof you’re more than “background noise”?
It feels… forced. Like I’d just be pretending. But I guess I could try noticing, without writing it down or anything.

That’s a good starting point—just paying attention without pressure. Noticing can gently shift how you view yourself over time. Would you like me to help you identify ways to spot those moments in everyday life?
I guess I keep going back to that moment because it’s proof I haven’t changed. But maybe… it’s also why I need to.
It’s insightful that you see both the weight and the motivation in that moment. Recognizing the need for change is a strong first step toward it. What small change feels doable for you right now?
I could try to just notice when I’ve made a small difference—like with the trash thing. It feels manageable, at least.
That sounds like a healthy and realistic goal. Even small differences can slowly build a sense of visibility and value. Would you like to set a timeframe for trying this so it feels more intentional?
Is noticing really enough, though? It feels too simple to make a difference.

Noticing is a starting point—it can soften old, harsh beliefs and make room for change. From there, small actions and reflections can gradually strengthen new patterns. Would you be open to pairing noticing with one intentional act of connection each week?
I appreciate the suggestion, but I’m not sure I can take on anything more than just noticing for now. It already feels like a lot.
That’s completely okay—starting small can be powerful and sustainable. Noticing alone can build awareness and gently shift how you see yourself. Would you like to check in later about how it’s going?
Yeah, checking in later might help. It’ll keep me honest with myself.
That sounds like a good plan. We can revisit what you’ve noticed and how it feels over time. When would you like to set that check-in?
I could just set a reminder for next Sunday around this time—same day, same hour. That should work.

Perfect, setting a clear reminder can help make it feel consistent. Next Sunday we can reflect on any moments you noticed and how they affected you. How do you feel about ending today’s conversation here?
Thanks for listening. I appreciate that you didn’t push me to do more than I can handle.
You’re welcome, and I’m glad you felt supported at your own pace. Taking it step by step is how meaningful change often begins. I’ll be here next Sunday to check in with you.
